Polite: 주문해요. Past: 주문했어요.

en: we / our — and "my" for shared things

회사 (company) + 원 (member) — you already own half this word.
요리 + 사 (professional). Same -사 as in 의사.

The 말 in 반말 ("half-speech") and 한국말 (colloquial for 한국어).
Polite: 살아요. Where you live takes 에: 한국에 살아요.
말 + 하다. Polite: 말해요.
Polite: 알아요 — also the everyday "got it / I see."
Polite: 몰라요 (mollayo) — a 르-irregular like 배불러요. Its own word, not 안 알다.

있다 for respected people. Polite: 계세요.
Polite: 바빠요 — the ㅡ drops, same as 배고프다 → 배고파요.
Polite: 친절해요.
안녕하세요 with the politeness stripped off — friends only.
The all-purpose formal apology — also "excuse me" when squeezing past someone.
The ladder: 죄송합니다 → 미안해요 → 미안 (friends).
Literally "having met you, I'm glad" — and your first 합니다-style phrase in the wild.

네 명 (four people). The honorific version is 분.
Also for fish on a plate: 생선 두 마리.
Always with native numbers: 열 살, 스무 살.

SINO numbers: 십 분 (10 minutes). Hours native, minutes Sino — the hybrid clock.
커피 한 잔, 물 두 잔.
맥주 두 병. Also the standalone word for "bottle."
책 세 권 (three books).

대답해요. 질문's other half.

단어's partner. This module completes your beginner 문법 engine.
무슨 뜻이에요? — what does it mean? Your dictionary-replacement sentence.

The 잘 in 잘 먹겠습니다 and 잘 지냈어요 — now a free agent: 잘 자요 (sleep well), 잘 못 해요 (can't do it well).
열심히 공부해요 — THE Korean study adverb. Literally 'with a burning heart.'

오래 기다렸어요? — did you wait long? (Say 아니요 even if you did.)

바람이 불어요 — the wind blows.

Same word family as 'typhoon' — both from Chinese 台風.
70% of Korea. Fall 산 + 단풍 is a national pilgrimage.
바다에 가요 covers 'go to the beach' — no separate word needed yet.
벚 (cherry) + 꽃 (M7's flower). Two weeks of national festival every spring.
The red-gold autumn leaves — and the maple they come from.
여름 휴가 — the sacred summer week.
학 (study) released — 방학. Work takes 휴가, school takes 방학.
여행을 가다 — go on a trip. Module 23 makes a whole journey of it.
스키를 타다 — ride skis, like every vehicle since M6.
눈 (snow) + 사람 (M1's person). You've been able to decode this since Module 1 — now it's official.
Konglish, clipped from 'air conditioner.' Summer's most beloved appliance.
바람이 불어요. Also blowing out candles, playing wind instruments.
비가 그쳤어요 — the rain stopped. Weather stops itself; no one stops it.
더워요 — ㅂ-irregular, and this module makes the whole family official.
추워요. Weather is 덥다/춥다; things (coffee, hands) use different words — later.
흐려요 — regular, mercifully.
맑아요 (말가요 by liaison). The batchim ㄺ reads ㄱ alone: 맑다 = 막따.
습해요. The 장마 special.
건조해요. Korean winters are famously 건조하다 — hence the humidifiers.
아주 더워요 — very hot. The neutral 'very.'
Officially 'excessively,' colloquially just 'so': 너무 좋아요 — I love it.
진짜요? — really?! Conversational gold. Its formal twin is 정말.
정말 감사합니다 — thank you so much. 진짜's slightly dressier sibling.
얼마나 더워요? — how hot is it? 얼마 (M9) grown an -나 and asking about degree.
The intercity kind; the KTX is Korea's bullet 기차.
비행 (flight) + 기 (machine). 비행기를 타다 — like every vehicle.
The IOU from Module 6's 역 note, paid. 버스 정류장 in full.
기차표, 비행기표 — glue the vehicle on the front.
Physical roads and figurative ways alike — 길을 몰라요 works for both.
역 근처에 있어요 — it's near the station. A position noun in spirit, joins the M6 family.
기사 + 님 — how you address any taxi or bus driver. The gap deck explains the title system.
자리 있어요? — is this seat taken? (lit. does a spot exist?)
Subway meetups live and die by 출구 numbers: 삼 번 출구.
출구's mirror — 입 (enter) vs 출 (exit).
Sino numbers + 번: 삼 번 출구 (exit 3), 몇 번 버스? (which bus?). Also counts times — 한 번 (once, native).
서울역 — pronounced 서울력, a sound-interlude special (ㄴ-insertion).
Second city, first beaches. 서울에서 부산까지 — the classic KTX bracket.
쭉 가세요 — go straight. Also 'continuously' — 쭉 living somewhere.
Where the 파란불 (blue light = green light) from the gap deck lives.
버스 요금, 택시 요금 — what the 카드 taps away.
교통카드 — the tap-everywhere transit card (T-money) — is 교통 + M9's 카드.
막 (last) + 차 (M3's tea… no — the CAR sense!). The night's deadline; the gap deck explains its social physics.
The generic 'place': 좋은 곳 (a good place — parseable after M24). Not 곧 (soon, M10) — batchim differs.
The 지하 in 지하철 — now you own both halves. 지하 일 층 = B1.
갈아 (switch) + 타다 (M6's ride). 갈아타세요 — the transfer announcement you'll actually hear.
길을 건너요 — cross the street. Polite: 건너요.
은행을 지나요 — pass the bank. Also time passing: 시간이 지나요.
세워 주세요 — please pull over. The taxi phrase, powered by M9's do-for-me machine.
버스를 놓쳤어요 — the universal excuse. Polite: 놓쳐요.
길이 막혀요 — traffic is bad (lit. the road is blocked). The gap deck has the metaphor.
얼마나 걸려요? — how long does it take? 삼십 분 걸려요. Time gets 'caught' on the journey.
주차해요. 주차장 — parking lot (장 = place, as in 정류장).
조심하세요! — careful! What everyone says when you leave in bad weather.
빨라요 — 르-irregular, joining 몰라요/배불러요. The 빨리 in 빨리빨리 is its adverb.
느려요 — mercifully regular.
편해요. 편의점 (M6) is literally the 편-store — convenience made retail.
위험해요! Also on every warning sign: 위험.
빠르다's adverb — and doubled, it's the national tempo from the gap deck: 빨리빨리.
Konglish, from 'apartment.' Most of urban Korea lives in one — whole skylines of numbered towers.
거 (dwell) + 실 (room). The same 실 hides in 화장실 — and in 침실, two words down.
A rare final ㅋ. Alone it sounds like 부억; add 에서 and the ㅋ wakes up — 부엌에서 (bueokeseo). The sound interlude, live.
침 (sleep — the one in 침대) + 실 (room). The bed's room, literally.
The shoes-off zone every Korean home has. Guests stop here until waved in — and the street stays here too (see 온돌 in the gap deck).
Konglish 'veranda' — the glassed-in strip where the laundry dries and the plants live.
The surface you sit on — and in Korea, often sleep on. The gap deck's 온돌 explains why it's the warmest seat in the house.
Konglish, five syllables, and a typing-drill boss fight.
A counter, like M5's set — with Sino numbers: 일 층, 이 층. 몇 층이에요? works in every elevator in the country.
Konglish. The ㅍ is doing the 'f' work — Korean has no f, so ㅍ covers the shift.
냉 (cold) + 장 (storage) + 고 (warehouse): a cold-storage-warehouse. Korean names appliances by job description.
세탁 (laundry) + 기 (machine) — the same 기 as 비행기, the flying machine.
열다 (open — below) + 쇠 (metal): 'open-metal.' The word is a tiny job description.
Korea sorts it strictly — food waste (음식물) gets its own bin, its own bag, and its own smell politics.
Thick enough to sleep under ON the floor — the 온돌 lifestyle's essential kit (gap deck).
Watch the vowels: ㅔ then ㅐ — the merged-sound pair, both ways, in one word.
옷 (clothes — official in the clothes module) + 장 (storage — the one in 냉장고). A clothes-warehouse.
One word for fire and the lights. 불을 켜요 — turn it on. And M7's 파란불? That was this 불 all along.
Moving boxes, travel bags, anything hauled. 이삿짐 — moving-day 짐.
Lights, TV, 에어컨 — 켜다 flips anything on. Its opposite is two letters and one irregular: 끄다.
ㅡ-drop family (아프다, 바쁘다, 슬프다…): 끄 + 어요 → 꺼요. Two letters, full irregular pedigree.
문을 열어요. Its noun child is up in the vocab: 열쇠, the open-metal.
A law-abiding ㄷ — 닫아요, unlike 듣다/걷다. Not every ㄷ misbehaves.
이사 is the move itself. Point the destination with M6's (으)로: 새 집으로 이사해요.
정리 = order, arrangement. Desks, closets, photos, your life — all 정리-able.
쓰레기를 버리다 — the natural pair.
Doors, phones, sentences, habits — 고치다 repairs them all.
ㄼ batchim reads ㄹ before a consonant — 널따 — but both letters wake with a vowel: 넓어요 (neolbeoyo). The sound interlude's rule, running live.
Regular ㅂ, like 입다 — 좁아요, no ㅂ→우 magic. The irregular family doesn't take everyone.
ㄺ batchim like M11's 맑다: 박따 alone, 밝아요 (balgayo) once a vowel follows.
ㅂ-irregular: 어두워요. Joins the 덥다/춥다/맵다 family.
ㅂ-irregular: 더러워요. The anti-깨끗하다.
ㅂ-irregular: 시끄러워요. Shouted alone — 시끄러워! — it means 'keep it down!'
조용히 하세요 — the librarian's setting. A 하다-adjective, so no irregular surprises.
Clips onto the front of a noun, no glue needed: 새 집, 새 침대, 새 핸드폰. It never stands alone — always the 새 something.
이웃사촌 — 'neighbor-cousins': the saying that a close neighbor beats a distant relative.
After a plain noun (수업 전에) or a verb wearing -기 (자기 전에). 전 = the time before.
After a plain noun (수업 후에) or a verb stamped past with -(으)ㄴ (먹은 후에). 후 = the time after.
몸이 안 좋아요 — 'my body isn't good' — is how Korean says 'I'm unwell' without naming anything.
M11's snow, same syllable — the homograph finally lands its second job. 눈이 와요, snow comes; 눈이 아파요, your eye hurts. Context referees.
코가 막혀요 — a blocked nose runs on M12's 막히다, the traffic-jam verb. Sinus congestion is nasal traffic.
입이 무거워요 — a 'heavy mouth' keeps secrets. The gap deck has more body-idioms like it.
One word for both — 목이 아파요 covers sore throats and stiff necks; context decides which hurts.
Sounds exactly like Sino 팔 (eight, M2). You have two arms, not eight — 팔이 두 개.
Also 'bridge' — a river's legs. Two homographs in one module; the 눈 problem is everywhere.
손 (hand) has 손가락, finger; 발 has 발가락 — 'foot-fingers.' Korean names toes with perfect logic.
Final ㅍ — 무릅 alone, but 무릎이 (mureupi) wakes it with a vowel. 부엌's rule, new letter.
The part that hurts from desks and floors alike. 허리가 아파요 — half of Korea, daily.
코 + 피: nose-blood. In K-dramas, studying too hard always ends in 코피. One vowel from 커피 (coffee) — order carefully.
눈 + 물: eye-water. The body compounds itself from parts you own.
감기에 걸리다 — you get 'caught' by a cold. M12's 걸리다 moonlighting; the same verb hangs, catches, and takes time.
M5's ten, M13's 열다/열쇠 — and now body heat. 열이 있어요, there's a fever. The 열 syllable works three jobs.
기침을 해요 — coughing is something you 'do' in Korean.
병 (illness) + 원 (house) = 병원 — M6's hospital, finally decomposed. M5's bottle-counter 병 is a homograph; get well before you count bottles.
건강에 좋아요 — 'good for the health' — is printed on half the food packaging in Korea.
Konglish. 스트레스를 받다 — you 'receive' stress (M9's 받다, promoted to psychology); 풀다 unties it.
Konglish. Standard kit in 미세먼지 season (M11's fifth season) and cold season alike.
The thing every Korean kid fears at the 병원. 주사를 맞다 — you 'receive' a shot, verb arriving in a later module.
간호 (nursing) + the job-사 from 요리사 and 의사. M4's build-a-job machine still runs.
담배를 피우다 — see the verb below for the smoke-as-bloom poetry.
The ㅡ-drop family's patriarch finally enrolls: 아프 + 아요 → 아파요. You've been saying its shape since M3's 배고파요.

A NEW irregular family — ㅅ vanishes before vowels: 나 + 아요 → 나아요. Rare and mostly used to wish people well: 빨리 나으세요. Sounds identical to M7's 낮다 (low) — this module's homograph festival extends to sound-twins.
For the moment of injury — 다쳤어요, I got hurt. 아프다 is for the hurting after.
ㅂ-irregular: 누워요. The doctor's 여기에 누우세요 — lie down here — runs on it.
M12's 세우다 (stop the taxi) was this verb's causative cousin — 'make it stand.'
Literally 'to make bloom' — 꽃이 피다, flowers bloom. Korean gave smoking its grimmest poetry.
걱정 alone is the noun. 걱정하지 마세요 — the sentence this module exists for.
The toast, the birthday wish, the grandmother's sign-off: 건강하세요.
Darker on paper than in speech — casual Korean 'dies' of hunger, heat, and homework hourly. The gap deck explains 죽겠어요.
목 (throat) + 마르다 (dries): thirst is a drying throat. 르-family conjugation: 목말라요.
힘이 없어요 — no energy: the universal symptom. 힘내세요! — the universal encouragement.
푹 쉬세요, 푹 자요 — the adverb of proper rest. Doctors prescribe it verbatim.
아직 아파요 — still sick. With a negative it reads 'not yet': 아직 안 먹었어요.
초등 (beginning-level) + 학교. The ladder starts here: 초등 → 중 → 고등 → 대.
중 = middle — the same 중 as 중국 (the 'middle country,' China).
고등 = high-level. Shortened to 고등학생's 고교 in headlines — Korean compresses what it says often.
대 (big) + 학교: the big school. Casually just 대학.
대학 + 학생, overlapped into one word. Korean loves a shared syllable.
학 + 년 (year) — spelled 학년, said 항년: the sound interlude's nasalization rule, live. 몇 학년이에요?
학 (study) + 원 (the institute-원 of 병원). The second school day: most Korean kids go after regular school — math 학원, English 학원, piano 학원, taekwondo 학원.
M5's half, second job: your homeroom. 3학년 2반 — grade 3, class 2 — is how Korean schools address a kid.
교 (teach) + 실 (room) — the room-실 family from 화장실/침실/거실 goes to school.
The teach-과목-book. 교과서 같다 — 'like a textbook' — describes suspiciously perfect people.
공 (blank) + 책 (book): a blank-book. M1's 책 finally builds a compound.
연 (lead) + 필 (writing tool). 연필로 쓰세요 — M6's (으)로 marking the tool.
Konglish at its most efficient — one syllable, borrowed whole.
지우다 (to erase) + -개, the tool-maker suffix — M13's 베개 (lean-tool pillow) has a classmate. An eraser is an 'erase-tool.'
칠 (paint) + 판 (board) — a painted board.
교수 + the respect-님 of 선생님/기사님. Address professors with it always — M12's title system applies double on campus.
수 (number) + 학 (study-of). The -학 suffix names every field — watch for it.
Not M6's train-역 — a homograph syllable in the wild. Korea's 역사 runs five thousand years and one alphabet promulgation you've already read about.
그리다's noun — a drawing is 'a drawn.' The pair below.
외 (outside) + 국 (country) + 어 (language — the 어 of 한국어/영어/단어). You are, at this very moment, doing 외국어 공부.
점 (points) + 수 (number). 백 점 — a hundred points — is perfection; M9's 백 moonlights in report cards.
The noun inside M10's 대답하다. 정답 — the correct answer — is the quiz-show word.
처음 배워요 — learning for the first time. Also inside the formal first-meeting greeting 처음 뵙겠습니다.
처음's opposite number. 마지막 수업, 마지막 문제 — and M12's 막차 carries the same 막.
배우다's other half. 선생님이 가르쳐요, 학생이 배워요 — the classroom in two verbs.
단어를 외워요 — this app's entire business model in one verb.
Ask + see: 보다 rides along to soften it — 'ask and see.' Not M1's 물 — the 물 here is from 묻다, to inquire.
틀렸어요 — wrong answer. This app has been telling you this word's meaning every time you miss a quiz question.
맞아요! — you've heard it as 'that's right!' since forever. Also the receiving end of M14's 주사를 맞다.
Sounds exactly like 있다 (to exist) — 잊지 마세요 vs 있지요. Spelling tells them apart; context does the rest.
그림을 그려요 — draw a drawing. Korean happily pairs a verb with its own noun.
졸업 = graduation. February in Korea: graduation season, flowers everywhere. Said 조러파다 — ㅎ merges per the sound interlude.
Knock-knock — 똑똑 — is also the sound of knocking. A smart kid and a knocked door share an onomatopoeia.
The highest Korean compliment a grandmother can pay.
부지런하다's shadow. 르-family: 게을러요 — lazy even in conjugation, dropping letters.
힘 (M14's energy) + 들다 (costs): something that takes your strength. 힘들어요 — the honest answer to how studying is going.
사무 (office work) + 실 — the room-실 family (교실, 침실, 거실…) clocks in.
M10's 회의 + 실. By now you can name any room in the building.
무슨 직업이에요? — M10's 무슨 asking the small-talk classic.
직 (duty) + 원 (member — the one in 회사원). Also who you call over in any shop: 직원.
Konglish. 우리 팀 — M4's warm 우리 extends to the office.
The title ladder in one office: 사장님 above, 부장님 mid-floor — always with 님, never a bare name. M12's title system pays rent here.
기 (record) + 자 (person). The 기 of 일기 (diary) and, yes, 기차 tickets — busy syllable.
The job-사 family grows: 요리사, 간호사, 변호사. Hear -사 at a job's end and you can guess the shape.
Received with two hands, read carefully, placed on the table — never pocketed unread. The card IS the person; treat it accordingly.
Konglish. 메일 alone also works — Korean rarely means postal mail by it.
월 (month — the one starting 월요일) + 급 (pay): month-pay. 월급날 — payday — is a small national holiday.
출 (out — the one in 출구 and 출발) + 장. Going out on duty.
회 (gather — 회사/회의's 회) + 식 (eat — 식당's 식): the after-hours team dinner that is officially optional and practically not. Round two is 노래방.
평 (ordinary) + 일 (day): M2's 주말 finally gets its opposite.
이번 주, 이번 달, 이번 회의 — 'this current one.' M12's 번 (number/turn) behind it: this-turn.
The native month — 이번 달, 다음 달 — and also the moon in the sky. One 달 orbits, the other invoices.
M6 gave you here/there/over-there for PLACES — 이거/그거/저거 is the same trio for THINGS. 이거 주세요 has been waiting since M9.
그 = near the listener, like 거기. 그거 뭐예요? — what's that you've got?
저 = far from both, like 저기. Point across the room: 저거.
The enrolled-going verb: 회사에 다녀요, 학교에 다녀요, 학원에 다녀요. 가다 is one trip; 다니다 is a routine with your name on it.
출 (out) + 근 (duty): heading out to duty. Said 출그나다? No — 출근해요, straightforward.
퇴 (retreat) + 근 (duty): the day's sweetest verb. 퇴근했어요? doubles as evening small talk.
야 (night) + 근 (duty). The 근-family tells the whole workday: 출근, 퇴근, and when things go wrong, 야근.
Email, packages, texts, people to the airport — and time: 주말 잘 보내세요, 'send your weekend well.'
부탁 is the favor itself. 부탁해요 — please do this for me; 잘 부탁드립니다 — the formal 'I'm in your hands' that opens every working relationship in Korea.
M8's 끝나다 is 'it ends'; 끝내다 is 'I end it.' One vowel of agency: 일이 끝났어요 vs 일을 끝냈어요.
돈을 벌다 — the reason for all the 근-verbs above.
People, restaurants, yourself: 제 소개를 하겠습니다 opens a thousand first meetings. 소개해 주세요 — set me up (also, famously, with dates).
복사기 — the copy machine — adds M15's tool logic to the 기 of 세탁기.
M8's 늦다 is late in general; 지각 is the official offense, recorded and frowned upon. 지각하지 마세요.
M15's 틀리다 is wrong answers; 실수 is wrong actions. 실수했어요 — own it, then move on.
발표 = the presentation. Feared equally in 교실 and 회의실.
일을 그만뒀어요 — I quit my job. 그만! alone means 'stop it!' — parents' favorite syllables.
중요한 것? Coming in M17. For now: 회의가 중요해요.
Korean needs backwards: 돈이 필요해요 — 'money is needed (to me).' The wanter takes a back seat, 있어요-style.
